question: Can a compact, SDE-motivated feature law fitted to small mixture-of-experts runs predict final loss, divergence, and learning-rate-schedule rankings across model scale, training horizon, schedule family, continual pre-training, and fine-tuning?

key_findings.claim: Opt-Laws is an unusually accurate empirical schedule-ranking model on the reported MoE training stack.
key_findings.evidence: A 15-feature linear model plus intercept reaches held-out R-squared 0.998, 0.50% relative error, within-block Spearman 0.84, a 94% Top-2 hit rate, and regret 0.003 under configuration-level five-fold cross-validation. Its separate nonlinear divergence rule reaches F1 0.92 on 260 configurations, including 26 divergent runs.

key_findings.claim: The strongest extrapolation numbers come from a small, homogeneous, single-run test set and do not establish a universal optimization law.
key_findings.evidence: The 0.2% mean extrapolation error is computed on ten configurations using the same Skywork-style MoE family, AdamW settings, RedPajama data, tokenizer/batch setup, and final training-loss target as the calibration grid. Cross-family testing covers five groups and three smooth schedule families. No dense architecture, different optimizer, independent lab, repeated seed, error bar, or downstream capability is evaluated.

key_findings.claim: The printed Adam-SDE correspondence contains an algebraic parameter mismatch.
key_findings.evidence: The displayed Adam recurrence weights old momentum by 1-beta and the new gradient by beta, then declares beta=1-c-hat times eta and says beta is close to one. Euler discretization of the proposed SDE instead gives old-momentum coefficient 1-c-hat times eta and new-gradient coefficient c-hat times eta. Matching the displayed recurrence therefore requires beta=c-hat times eta, not 1-c-hat times eta; alternatively, the recurrence's beta labels must be swapped.

anchors.section: On the beta-eta coupling in Adam-SDE
B.1.2 Derivations for SGD-SDE and Adam-SDE

key_findings.claim: The Adam convergence assumptions and escape boundary conditions do not cover the empirical schedules used to motivate the feature law.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 relies on an infinite-horizon learning rate whose integral diverges while its squared integral converges. Every experiment uses a finite schedule that reaches zero, so extending it by zero makes the first integral finite. The escape theorems assume eta(0)=eta_max and eta(T)=0, while the empirical schedules start at zero and warm up; nevertheless, warmup derivative terms are included as escape features. The experiments also use fixed AdamW beta values, whereas the SDE couples beta to eta and calls the bridge an open problem.

anchors.section: On the beta-eta coupling in Adam-SDE

key_findings.claim: The random-matrix scaling used to motivate model-size dependence appears normalized in the wrong aspect ratio.
key_findings.evidence: The proof defines Z as an N-by-D matrix and the sample covariance as (1/D)ZZ-transpose, but centers its largest eigenvalue at 1+sqrt(D/N). For this normalization the Marchenko-Pastur upper edge depends on sqrt(N/D), with a square on the edge; the paper's expression corresponds to the opposite normalization/aspect ratio. The subsequent claim that D/N much greater than one inflates covariance therefore does not follow from the displayed sample covariance.

key_findings.claim: The theory motivates a feature vocabulary but does not derive final LLM loss from schedule geometry.
key_findings.evidence: The convergence results upper-bound a trajectory-averaged gradient norm, not the final cross-entropy. The paper invokes benign basins or a PL condition to connect this to loss but does not assume or verify PL for its models. The escape result is an anti-concentration bound for a local Gaussian linearization initialized exactly at a minimum; its big-O upper bound is then treated as a basin-quality feature. Exponents and unconstrained signed coefficients, including interaction powers absent from the theorems, are selected from data.

anchors.section: A.3 Exponent Selection and Fitted Coefficients

key_findings.claim: Continual-training and fine-tuning rankings are promising but too low-cardinality to validate the history-aware extension.
key_findings.evidence: The strong-shift study ranks three schedules, the weak-shift study five schedules whose observed losses span only 0.005, and fine-tuning ranks three candidates at each of three token budgets. The method gets most orders right, but these are selected candidates from one checkpoint and data pipeline; predicted scores are not calibrated losses in these stages, and no seed uncertainty is reported.

method.core_idea: Represent each learning-rate schedule by integrated learning-rate, squared-derivative, scale, and interaction features suggested by SDE convergence and local escape bounds, then fit a low-dimensional regression for final loss plus a separate divergence discriminant.
method.mechanism: A small MoE grid varies model size, token budget, peak rate, and warmup. Fifteen closed-form features summarize warmup and cooldown convergence mass, schedule-change energy, model/data scales, and mixed terms; exponents are discretely selected inside each training fold and coefficients fitted by linear regression. A history-aware variant accumulates integrated learning rate across pre-training stages while using only the current stage's normalized derivative feature.
assumptions: Final training loss is a stable, smooth function of a small schedule-feature basis within and beyond the calibration stack.
Trajectory-averaged gradient norm is a useful proxy for final cross-entropy despite no verified PL inequality.
Local Gaussian SDE anti-concentration near a minimum predicts which basin large-scale AdamW training selects.
Model/data dependence learned from one MoE family transfers to larger variants and later training stages.
Single-run loss differences are larger than initialization, data-order, and systems noise.
Schedules decay to zero and do not contain untested restarts, cycles, or nonzero terminal rates.

techniques.role: Encodes integrated learning-rate mass and squared schedule derivatives over selected phases.
Adds model-size, token-horizon, peak-rate, and pairwise convergence-escape interactions.
Selects exponent groups and regression coefficients using training configurations within each cross-validation fold.
Compares above-threshold rate exposure with effective warmup and scale to classify failed runs.
Carries accumulated optimization mass across pre-training, continual training, and fine-tuning.
Searches schedule parameters predicted to yield equal or low final loss before running them.

evaluations.setting: 260 Skywork-MoE pre-training configurations over seven model-size/token blocks; 234 convergent and 26 divergent.
evaluations.metric: Five-fold configuration-level R-squared, relative error, within-block Spearman, Top-2 hit rate, regret, and divergence F1.
evaluations.result: Generalized Opt-Laws reports 0.50% error, 0.84 Spearman, 94% Top-2, and divergence F1 0.92.
evaluations.baseline: Block mean, Chinchilla, raw linear regression, Tissue, simplified Opt-Laws plus Chinchilla scale, peak-rate threshold, and logistic regression.

evaluations.setting: Ten extrapolation configurations at 100B-300B tokens and up to a 4.05B-total-parameter MoE.
evaluations.metric: Mean relative final-loss error by single-phase, multiphase, and inverse-designed loss-equivalent groups.
evaluations.result: All reported errors are below 0.5%, with 0.2% mean versus 7.6%-50.8% for three fitted baselines.
evaluations.baseline: Raw linear regression, Tissue cross-scale, and simplified Opt-Laws with Chinchilla scale.

evaluations.setting: Five cross-family groups using linear, cosine, and constant-plus-linear cooldowns.
evaluations.metric: Final-loss error and whether the best schedule family is selected.
evaluations.result: The best family is selected in all five groups and each reported error is below 2%.
evaluations.baseline: Three schedule families evaluated after fitting only piecewise-linear schedules.

evaluations.setting: Continual pre-training from one 8-by-0.6B checkpoint on 100B Chinese or English tokens.
evaluations.metric: Rank of three strong-shift and five weak-shift schedules.
evaluations.result: The exact strong-shift ranking and weak-shift ranks three through five are recovered; the two near-tied leaders are reversed.
evaluations.baseline: Observed final loss of each candidate schedule.

evaluations.setting: Java-code fine-tuning after English pre-training and Chinese continual training, at 3B, 30B, and 60B tokens.
evaluations.metric: Rank among three candidates at each budget.
evaluations.result: All nine candidate ranks match, including one two-phase schedule at 60B.

limitations: Empirical coverage is confined to one related MoE architecture family, AdamW stack, data pipeline, and cross-entropy objective.
No repeated seeds, uncertainty intervals, or noise floor are supplied for sub-percent loss differences.
The ten-point extrapolation and low-cardinality continual/fine-tuning rankings are too small for broad scaling claims.
Held-out grid folds interpolate peak-rate and warmup configurations inside every model/token block rather than holding out whole scales.
The Adam-SDE parameter mapping is inconsistent with the displayed Adam recurrence, and its learning-rate assumptions exclude the experimental finite schedules.
The random-matrix aspect ratio in Proposition 3 is inconsistent with the displayed sample-covariance normalization.
The feature law is fit to final training loss, not validation loss, downstream quality, forgetting, or compute-normalized utility.
Only zero-terminal, smooth noncyclic schedules are covered; fixed, restart, cyclic, and nonzero-terminal policies are outside scope.
Exponent search and unconstrained signed coefficients make the generalized model less physically interpretable than its SDE narrative suggests.
failure_modes: A schedule selected on predicted differences smaller than run-to-run noise is not actually better on rerun.
A dense model or different MoE router changes scale interactions and invalidates fitted coefficients.
A nonzero terminal rate or warm restart makes derivative and convergence features fall outside the theory and calibration set.
Distribution shift changes irreducible loss or forgetting dynamics that accumulated learning-rate mass cannot represent.
A schedule attains low training loss but worse validation, capability retention, or downstream performance.
The divergence boundary fails when gradient clipping, batch size, optimizer state, or numerical precision changes.
Correlated basis terms yield unstable signed coefficients while aggregate in-grid predictions remain deceptively accurate.
reusable_insights: Evaluate schedule predictors with within-scale ranking and regret; aggregate R-squared can be dominated by model and token scale.
Treat integrated learning rate and schedule-change energy as useful empirical descriptors even when the mechanistic SDE story is uncertain.
Hold out whole architectures, optimizers, datasets, and scale blocks before calling a regression a general optimization law.
Repeat promising schedules enough times to estimate whether predicted sub-percent improvements exceed the training noise floor.
Separate theorem-valid features from empirically added interactions and document every assumption broken by the production optimizer.
Prospective inverse design is a stronger test than retrospective fitting, but candidate-selection and replication uncertainty must still be reported.
open_questions: Do coefficients transfer to dense transformers, non-language modalities, different tokenizers, and optimizers such as Muon or Adafactor?
What is the run-to-run variance of final loss at the schedule differences Opt-Laws aims to resolve?
Can the Adam recurrence/SDE mapping and sample-covariance random-matrix scaling be repaired without changing the feature basis?
Can a finite-horizon theorem directly cover zero-to-peak warmup, fixed Adam betas, decoupled weight decay, clipping, and zero cooldown?
Does schedule ranking remain accurate for validation loss, downstream accuracy, forgetting, and safety rather than training loss alone?
How does blockwise scale holdout compare with configuration interpolation under the same calibration compute?
Can uncertainty-aware active design choose the next small runs and abstain when candidate schedules are statistically tied?

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Law with Learning Rate Annealing
competitive_landscape.difference: Tissue et al. predict the full loss curve from cumulative learning-rate area and annealing area with fewer terms; Opt-Laws targets final loss and adds SDE-motivated escape and cross-scale interactions, winning on its grid at the cost of more fitted structure.

competitive_landscape.title: A Multi-Power Law for Loss Curve Prediction Across Learning Rate Schedules
competitive_landscape.difference: The ICLR 2025 multi-power law predicts every intermediate loss across constant, cosine, and step schedules and optimizes a new schedule; Opt-Laws instead predicts final loss, divergence, and later-stage rankings with a richer MoE-specific feature regression.

competitive_landscape.title: Unveiling the Role of Learning Rate Schedules via Functional Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Functional Scaling Laws model population-risk trajectories through intrinsic time and SGD theory, then test 0.1B-1B LLMs; they offer a more direct loss-dynamics bridge than Opt-Laws' local-minimum anti-concentration heuristic.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Dynamics in Continual Pre-Training for Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. explicitly decouple distribution shift and learning-rate annealing to predict validation-loss trajectories throughout continual pre-training; Opt-Laws accumulates optimization history but ranks only a few final training losses.

competitive_landscape.title: A Hitchhiker's Guide to Scaling Law Estimation
competitive_landscape.difference: Choshen et al. study fitting, extrapolation, and interpretation failure modes for scaling laws, supplying the uncertainty and protocol perspective needed to test whether Opt-Laws' sub-percent predictions survive seeds and domain holdouts.

competitive_landscape.title: Optimal Learning Rate Schedules under Functional Scaling Laws: Power Decay and Warmup-Stable-Decay
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. analytically characterize optimal power-decay versus WSD-like schedules by task regime under a functional scaling law, whereas Opt-Laws numerically ranks candidates through fitted schedule integrals.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Opt-Laws is an SDE-grounded, interpretable optimization hyper-parameter law that predicts large-scale LLM loss and selects near-optimal schedules across pre-training, continual training, and fine-tuning from small runs.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The reported MoE grid has strong held-out ranking metrics, a separate divergence benchmark, prospective loss-equivalent schedules, cross-family tests, and correct low-cardinality later-stage rankings.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The combination of within-block selection metrics, divergence modeling, history-aware features, and prospective schedule design is useful and empirically strong. It is best understood as a high-performing surrogate for one training stack, not yet a law derived from the SDEs: two mathematical mappings are inconsistent, theorem assumptions miss the production schedules and AdamW dynamics, and the spectacular sub-percent extrapolation lacks seed uncertainty and architecture/data holdouts.

reviewer_notes: Read all 60 pages, including every proof, coefficient table, ablation, scope statement, and reference page. Visually inspected Tables 1-5, 8, 10, and 13, Figure 7, and the displayed covariance and escape equations to resolve extraction layout and verify the Adam-beta and Marchenko-Pastur normalization contradictions. Primary OpenReview, arXiv, and PMLR competitors were checked on 2026-08-23.
